explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Rehoboam, Solomon's son, mobilizes Judah and Benjamin, 180,000 chosen warriors, to fight Israel and restore the kingdom to himself (2 Chronicles 11:1). Some of us answer a rough day with a nap. This man answers with a draft notice for 180,000. Hold onto that number, because the LORD has something to say about it.

Not quite, friend. The text says Rehoboam arrives in Jerusalem and mobilizes the house of Judah and Benjamin, 180,000 chosen warriors, to fight against Israel (2 Chronicles 11:1). He wants the kingdom restored to him, and he doesn't plan on asking nicely. I think Rehoboam was NOT in a talking mood.

That's it. The word of the LORD comes to Shemaiah, a man of God, and it says, “You are not to go up and fight against your brothers.” (2 Chronicles 11:4). Picture 180,000 warriors, boots laced, and a message arrives that says to stand down. I'd have asked if there was a second page.

Nope, friend. The message doesn't send anybody marching. It says, “You are not to go up and fight against your brothers.” (2 Chronicles 11:4). Early starts are great for baking, but this message is about staying put.

explanations.answer: Wait for a sign then attack
explanations.explanation: Close to a plan, friend, but there's no sign and no attack in this message. The LORD says, “You are not to go up and fight against your brothers.” (2 Chronicles 11:4). The answer is already given, and it's a no to the fight. The warriors didn't need to keep watching the sky.

You got it, baker. The LORD says, “Each of you must return home, for this is My doing.” (2 Chronicles 11:4). That's the reason, and it's the one He gives. No strategy talk, no battle math. When He gives the reason, that's the whole reason.

Good guess, friend, but the message says nothing about how strong anybody is. The reason the LORD gives is, “…for this is My doing.” (2 Chronicles 11:4). Rehoboam had 180,000 warriors ready, and the LORD still didn't talk about odds. He pointed to His own doing.

That would be a fine reason in a gym, friend, but it isn't in the text. The LORD's reason is, “…for this is My doing.” (2 Chronicles 11:4). Nobody gets sent home for a skills check here. The warriors were chosen warriors already (2 Chronicles 11:1).

Not this time, friend. The text says the opposite: they listened to the words of the LORD and turned back from going against Jeroboam (2 Chronicles 11:4). Jeroboam was the man they had been set to go against. 180,000 warriors turned around, and I think that took real discipline. Nobody wants to be the one who says, "Well, we're already dressed."

Right, friend. They listened to the words of the LORD and turned back from going against Jeroboam, the man the army was set to go against (2 Chronicles 11:4). No marching and no sneaking out the back. A whole army heard the message and went home. That's a lot of people agreeing on the same day.

Yes, friend. Rehoboam lives in Jerusalem and builds up cities for defense in Judah (2 Chronicles 11:5). Later we see officers, supplies, shields and spears in them (2 Chronicles 11:11-12). Every one of those details points the same way. He's making Judah hard to get into.

Reasonable guess, friend, since cities do trade. But the text says these cities were built up for defense (2 Chronicles 11:5). Then it lists officers, supplies, shields and spears (2 Chronicles 11:11-12). That's a lot of spears for a shopping district.

Good heart on that answer, friend, but it isn't what the text says. Rehoboam builds up cities in Judah for defense (2 Chronicles 11:5). You can see it in the officers, supplies, shields and spears he adds (2 Chronicles 11:11-12). Those are things you stack for protection.

That's the one. Rehoboam puts shields and spears in all the cities and strengthens them greatly (2 Chronicles 11:12). Add that to the officers and the supplies of food, oil and wine in verse 11, and each city has a full kit. Fifteen cities is a lot of shields to count.

That's a good thing for a military, friend, but the text doesn't list them here. What Rehoboam puts in all the cities is shields and spears (2 Chronicles 11:12). I think he was keeping it simple. Simple still takes a LOT of spears.

Close to the idea of a well-stocked city, friend, but gold and silver aren't mentioned. The text says Rehoboam puts shields and spears in all of them (2 Chronicles 11:12). Along with the officers and supplies, that's the full list for this verse. Shields and spears were the decor.

That's right. The priests and Levites from all their districts throughout Israel stood with Rehoboam (2 Chronicles 11:13). That's a big group walking toward Judah. And the next verse tells us what pushed them out of their homes.

Not this time, friend. The text says the priests and Levites from all their districts throughout Israel stood with Rehoboam (2 Chronicles 11:13). The Gibeonites aren't in this passage at all. Watch for the priests and the Levites, because verse 14 is all about them.

Fair try, friend, but the Kenites aren't mentioned here. The text names the priests and Levites from all their districts throughout Israel (2 Chronicles 11:13). They're the ones who stand with Rehoboam. You'll see why they left in the very next verse.

Yes, friend. Jeroboam and his sons rejected them as priests of the LORD, so the Levites left their pasturelands and possessions and went to Judah and Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 11:14). They left everything behind. Packing up your whole life takes more than a Saturday and a borrowed truck.

That would've kept everybody home, friend. The text says Jeroboam and his sons rejected the Levites as priests of the LORD, and that's why they went to Judah and Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 11:14). Then Jeroboam appointed his own priests (2 Chronicles 11:15). Nobody leaves their pastureland over a warm welcome.

Nice thought, friend, but anointing isn't what happened. The text says Jeroboam and his sons rejected the Levites as priests of the LORD (2 Chronicles 11:14). The Levites then left their pasturelands and possessions for Judah and Jerusalem. They were pushed out of the job, not given a promotion.

explanations.answer: People from every tribe seeking the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's it. Those from every tribe of Israel who had set their hearts to seek the LORD their God followed the Levites to Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 11:16). It starts with the Levites, and then regular folks follow. I think that's a mighty long walk with your heart set.

explanations.answer: Soldiers from every tribe seeking pay
explanations.explanation: Interesting, friend, but pay isn't in the text. The people who followed the Levites were those from every tribe who had set their hearts to seek the LORD their God (2 Chronicles 11:16). They came for the LORD. No paycheck was mentioned.

explanations.answer: Merchants from every tribe seeking trade
explanations.explanation: Good business sense, friend, but that isn't what the text says. Those who followed were from every tribe of Israel, and they had set their hearts to seek the LORD their God (2 Chronicles 11:16). They traveled to Jerusalem to sacrifice to Him. Nobody set up a booth.

True, friend. They followed the Levites to Jerusalem “…to sacrifice to the LORD, the God of their fathers.” (2 Chronicles 11:16). They didn't come for a tour. They came to bring their sacrifices to the LORD.

Not false, friend. The text says they came to Jerusalem “…to sacrifice to the LORD, the God of their fathers.” (2 Chronicles 11:16). These were people who had set their hearts to seek Him. Their reason for the trip is right there in the verse.

Yes, friend. They supported Rehoboam for three years because they walked for three years in the way of David and Solomon (2 Chronicles 11:17). David was Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3). The support has a reason, and it's the way they walked. It's also a stretch of three years, and that's all it says.

Not this one, friend. The text names David, not Saul. Saul was Israel's first king (1 Samuel 11:15), but the verse says they walked for three years in the way of David and Solomon (2 Chronicles 11:17). Keep an eye on David's name in this chapter.

Good name, friend, but it isn't the one in this verse. Moses was Israel's leader, and the text here says they walked for three years in the way of David and Solomon (2 Chronicles 11:17). It's about the way of those two kings. Three years is what the verse gives.

That's him. Rehoboam appoints Abijah son of Maacah as chief prince among his brothers (2 Chronicles 11:22). Maacah is the wife he loved more than all the rest (2 Chronicles 11:21). I think that's a pretty big hint, but the text just tells us what he did. Twenty-eight sons, and one gets the title.

Good try, friend. Jeush is one of the sons Mahalath bore to Rehoboam (2 Chronicles 11:19), but he isn't the one named chief prince. That's Abijah son of Maacah (2 Chronicles 11:22). With twenty-eight sons, the names pile up fast.

Close family, friend, wrong brother. Zaham is another son of Mahalath (2 Chronicles 11:19), and Rehoboam appoints someone else as chief prince. It's Abijah son of Maacah (2 Chronicles 11:22). Tracking this family tree takes an apron full of notes.

Not quite, friend. The text says Rehoboam appointed Abijah as chief prince among his brothers, intending to make him king (2 Chronicles 11:22). So Abijah is the one he has in mind for the throne. The title and the plan point to the same son.

Yes, friend. Rehoboam appointed Abijah son of Maacah as chief prince, “…intending to make him king.” (2 Chronicles 11:22). There's no other son in the plan. In this house, the plan and the title belong to one boy.

explanations.answer: Spreads them through the fortified cities
explanations.explanation: That's the wise move. Rehoboam disperses some of his sons throughout the districts of Judah and Benjamin, and to all the fortified cities (2 Chronicles 11:23). The text itself calls it acting wisely. I think the family reunion got a lot more spread out.

That's the opposite, friend. The text says he dispersed some of his sons throughout the districts of Judah and Benjamin, and to all the fortified cities (2 Chronicles 11:23). They didn't stay together in one place. He sent them out.

explanations.answer: Sends them off to serve Pharaoh
explanations.explanation: Not at all, friend. Pharaoh, Egypt's king, isn't anywhere in this passage. The text says Rehoboam dispersed some of his sons throughout the districts of Judah and Benjamin, and to all the fortified cities (2 Chronicles 11:23). They stayed in his own kingdom.
